Let set \(A\) and set \(B\) represent collections of lower-case letters:

\[A=\{j,\,u,\,s,\,y,\,g,\,a,\,v,\,i,\,p,\,z\}\] \[B=\{x,\,i,\,s,\,m,\,n\}\]

Calculate the following cardinalities:

  • \(n(A)=\)
  • \(n(B)=\)
  • \(n(A\cap B)=\)
  • \(n(A\cup B)=\)

Set \(A\) has 10 elements. \[n(A)=10\]

Set \(B\) has 5 elements. \[n(B)=5\]

Next, identify the intersection. What elements are common to both sets?

\[A\cap B ~=~ \{s,\,i\}\]

Set \(A\cap B\) has 2 elements. \[n(A\cap B)=2\]

Next, you could try writing out all elements of the union.

\[A\cup B ~=~ \{g,\,a,\,n,\,s,\,x,\,j,\,y,\,v,\,p,\,i,\,m,\,u,\,z\}\]

However, it is probably easier to use the inclusion-exclusion principle:

\[n(A\cup B)~=~n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\] \[n(A\cup B)~=~10+5-2\] \[n(A\cup B)~=~13\]

Let set \(S\) represent a collection of lower-case letters:

\[S=\{y,\,s,\,l,\,b,\,h,\,g,\,k,\,t,\,a\}\]

Calculate the number of proper subsets of \(S\).

Set \(S\) has 9 elements.

\[n(S)~=~9\]

The formula for the number of subsets is \(2^{n(S)}\). But that includes \(S\), which is not a proper subset of itself, so we need to subtract 1 to find the number of proper subsets.

\[2^{9}-1=511\]

We could get fancy...

\[n(\{A|A\subset S\})~=~2^{n(S)}-1\]

Let \(p\) represent the quantified logical statement below.

\[p: \text{ Some owls are green.}\]

Which of the following represents the negation of \(p\)? In other words, which represents \(\sim p\)?

Let set \(A\) represent the set of all things classified as owls.

Let set \(B\) represent the set of all things classified as green.

Statement \(p\) says that the intersection of \(A\) and \(B\) is not empty.

The logical negation, \(\sim p\) would be that \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint.

Thus,

\[\sim p: \text{ No owls are green.}\]

\[p: \text{ No apples are enigmatic.}\]

Let set \(A\) represent the set of all things classified as apples.

Let set \(B\) represent the set of all things classified as enigmatic.

The logical negation, \(\sim p\) would be that the intersection of \(A\) and \(B\) is not empty.

Thus,

\[\sim p: \text{ Some apples are enigmatic.}\]

A conditional statement is stated below:

  2. If umbrellas are green, then bugs are NOT enigmatic.
  3. If umbrellas are NOT green, then bugs are enigmatic.
  • Which variation is logically equivalent to the original?

If the original conditional statement is \(p\to q\), then:

  • Contrapositive is \(\sim q \to \sim p\)
  • Converse is \(q \to p\)
  • Inverse is \(\sim p \to \sim q\)

And the contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original conditional statement.

In this case the original conditional statement was:

  • If bugs are enigmatic, then umbrellas are NOT green.
  • The contrapositive would be:
    • If umbrellas are green, then bugs are NOT enigmatic.
  • The converse would be:
    • If umbrellas are NOT green, then bugs are enigmatic.
  • The inverse would be:
    • If bugs are NOT enigmatic, then umbrellas are green.

Thus, (1) is the inverse, and (2) is the contrapositive, and (3) is the converse. And so (2) is the logically equivalent statement.
